newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK govt to cool property boom with supply-analysts.
newsitem.headline: HK govt to cool property boom with supply-analysts.

text.p: Hong Kong's future government is likely to resort to an increase in land supply and not the introduction of new taxes to curb soaring residential prices, property analysts said on Wednesday.

A move is widely expected soon after Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule on midnight of June 30 and real estate tycoon C.Y. Leung, head of a post-colonial committee to map out housing strategy, has recently completed a report outlining his ideas.

"C.Y. Leung is not the kind of person that would want to advocate dramatic interference in the free market. What he is more likely to look at is increasing supply," said Martin Tacon, senior associate at CS First Boston.
"I expect to see initiatives to increase affordable housing and also try and push through reforms on urban redevelopment."
Leung has yet to detail his proposals, but speculation surrounding their content has already dampened the property market, where prices have risen almost 30 percent this year.
Analysts said the new government was likely to release more land for development and could speed up procedures that have to be completed before a site can be developed.
"The only thing that is ultimately effective is going to be to increase supply and do it quickly," said Peter Churchouse, managing director at Morgan Stanley Asia.

While increased supply could create a "slight downdraft in the residential property market" in the near term, real demand and a buoyant economy would drive the market in the longer term protecting property developers' earnings, he said.

"If the government does what I am expecting, predominantly supply side, that will not affect earnings for developers short term to medium term," said Tacon. "The best they can do is create a stable environment - property prices going up in line with inflation would be an ideal scenario."
Churchouse said if the supply of housing to be built by the private sector doubled compared to last year, major property developers could still see a 24 percent increase in net profit.
"Property prices will have to fall at least 30 percent for developers' profit to be heading into negative territory, and that is somewhat unlikely," Churchouse added.
Analysts expected no drastic measures on the demand side.
"I think the government's goal is clearly to increase the amount of housing and demand side measures don't do that. All they do is control prices," said Tacon.

Churchouse said the impact of demand-side measures would not be long-lasting. "I think suppressing demand is a bit like pushing a jack in the box -- you know you push it down but it's going to spring back up again in a few months."

While the government might increase stamp duties or step up rules on how developers release apartments for sale, he did not expect the government to introduce new types of taxes, such as a capital gains tax, which would contradict the territory's philosophy of a simple tax system with low taxes.
"I think all it has to do is implement the existing legislation on profit tax," Churchouse said, adding that speculators trading properties should be taxed as businesses.

Experience suggested the introduction of stamp duty would do little to cool the property sector, he said. "It's not going to end speculative activity. I think it is a hopeless thing to do. I don't think it's effective at all."
Analysts said Tung's government, which will be brought in on Hong Kong's reversion to China on July 1, would aim at maintaining an orderly market instead of crushing the sector.
While Churchouse saw some short-term weakness if measures were imposed, he predicted average home prices would still be up 15-20 percent by year-end 1997 over year-end 1996.
